title: Olympiad Day 9: Uzbekistan takes a giant step towards gold
summary: India stays in the hunt, while a surprise victory by Uzbekistan’s second team shakes up the race With just two rounds remaining, the race at the top has become increasingly unpredictable. Uzbekistan took a major step towards gold by defeating the United States, while India kept its hopes alive with a crucial victory over Germany, led by Gukesh’s win on board four. France and China shared all four points, while Uzbekistan’s second team produced the biggest surprise of the day with a crushing 3.5–0.5 victory over sixth-seeded Netherlands. Armenia, Hungary, Spain and Ukraine also picked up important wins to remain in the mix, setting up a fascinating final two rounds in which almost anything can still happen. In the Women’s section, China strengthened their grip on first place with a 3-1 victory over Armenia, led by key wins from Lu Miaoyi and Zhu Jiner, while India moved into the medal zone by defeating hosts Uzbekistan 3-1, with Divya Deshmukh and Vantika Agrawal both remaining undefeated. Full results 46th Chess Olympiad Let’s take a closer look at the action from the playing hall. Ceremonial moves add a touch of showmanship One of this afternoon’s ceremonial moves came with a twist. Simon Belanger, the internationally renowned chess content creator known for his outstanding Magnus Carlsen impressions, opened the game for Aksel Bu Kvaløy, board four of the Norway – Philippines match. His choice of 1.f3, delivered alongside his trademark Carlsen impression, was greeted with laughter and a round of applause from those watching. The ceremonial moves continued with José Antonio Carrillo, President of the Confederation of Chess for the Americas, making the first move for Cuba’s second board in their match against Poland. Alisher Muminov, founder of the “Sky Chess” Academy, then opened the game for Gulrukhbegim Tokhirjonova in her match against Divya Deshmukh in the Uzbekistan–India encounter. Finally, the action moved to one of the day’s most important matches, Uzbekistan versus the United States. Saydali  Yuldashev, Manager of the Uzbekistan Men’s National Chess Team, made the ceremonial first move for Nodirbek Abdusattorov, choosing the popular 1.b3. Open section Uzbekistan takes a giant step towards gold Each day that goes by makes it more difficult to predict who will ultimately take the gold. Yesterday, Germany defeated Uzbekistan, putting themselves firmly into contention, but today the picture changed dramatically. India overcame Germany, while Uzbekistan bounced back, defeating the United States and taking a major step towards the top of the standings. What will happen tomorrow? It is anyone’s guess, but Uzbekistan’s position is looking increasingly strong. The first game to finish was on board four, where Aronian and Madaminov played out an absolutely level game. Madaminov defended with impressive simplicity against the legendary former Armenian, neutralising any danger and securing the draw. The other three games went all the way to the limit. Fabiano Caruana appeared to have the draw firmly in hand but decided against exchanging a pair of rooks, allowing the game to enter a double-rook endgame against Nodirbek Abdusattorov. The Uzbek star, still undefeated with 7/9, eventually converted his chances. At this rate, he is firmly in contention for the individual gold medal on board one. On board two, Wesley So handed Javokhir Sindarov his first defeat of the Olympiad after outplaying him in a fine technical game. Everything came down to the final game between Nodirbek Yakubboev and Hans Niemann. In a difficult position, the American sacrificed a piece for three pawns, but the compensation proved insufficient. Yakubboev held on to win, completing another victory for the Uzbek team. Once again, the combined force of the two Nodirbeks had delivered for Uzbekistan. Gukesh keeps India’s gold hopes alive The other key match of the day, between Germany and India, turned out very differently. Trailing by one match point, India needed a victory to keep their gold-medal hopes alive. The first three boards all ended in draws after more or less accurate play, but on board four, Gukesh D came under serious pressure against Alexander Donchenko. However, with time running short, Donchenko lost his way in the tactical complications, allowing the World Champion to turn the tables and score a decisive victory. It was a crucial point for India’s team ambitions and another important result for Gukesh’s individual medal campaign: he remains undefeated on 7.5/9. After the game, Gukesh kindly accepted our request to analyse the encounter for the fans, taking the time to explain the key moments and ideas from the game. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1HDYvk42C64 Uzbekistan’s second team stuns the Netherlands France and China drew all four games, although Wei Yi was fortunate to escape with a draw in a difficult position. The result keeps both teams’ medal hopes alive, but the biggest surprise of the afternoon came from Uzbekistan’s second team, which produced a stunning 3.5–0.5 victory over sixth-seeded Netherlands. The result leaves the strong Dutch team with little room to manoeuvre in the medal race with just two rounds remaining. Seeded 30th, Uzbekistan’s second team has been one of the revelations of the Olympiad. And with the host nation’s third team also performing exceptionally well, the lower-seeded Uzbek side could yet play a decisive role in shaping the final standings over the last two rounds. Armenia, Hungary, Spain and Ukraine keep their hopes alive Other important results saw Armenia prevail over Azerbaijan 2.5–1.5, while Hungary defeated Austria 3–1 to move back into contention after a wobbly middle section of the tournament. Spain and Ukraine also kept their outside chances of a top-five finish alive, beating the Czech Republic 3–1 and Georgia 2.5–1.5 respectively. Women’s Section China extends its lead China extended its lead in the standings with a convincing 3-1 victory over Armenia. They now sit two full match points clear of India, Kazakhstan and Mongolia, with only India boasting a comparable tiebreak. After solid draws on boards two and four, Lu Miaoyi once again demonstrated her tactical skills, scoring the key win for China. title: ChessMom returns in Samarkand: Supporting mothers on and off the board
summary: The ChessMom Project has doubled in size since its debut in Budapest, giving 12 players the opportunity to compete at the 2026 Chess Olympiad while travelling with their young children and caregivers. When the 46th Chess Olympiad got underway in Samarkand, more than 3,000 players, captains and officials from around the world came together for one of the biggest events worldwide. After team Angola was finally able to join for the third round, the confirmed official numbers are outstanding: 205 open and 189 women teams. A record number of teams and the biggest FIDE Chess Olympiad in history! Among them are a group of players whose challenge extends beyond the chessboard: they are competing at the highest level while also caring for very young children. An Olympiad is an intense three-week experience. Players spend long hours preparing, competing and recovering between rounds, often travelling thousands of kilometres from home. For a mother with a baby or toddler, those demands add another layer of organisation to an already rigorous professional environment. The ChessMom Project is designed to remove at least one of those barriers: the need to choose between being present for one’s child and representing one’s country on the international chess stage. Launched as a pilot initiative at the 2024 Chess Olympiad in Budapest, ChessMom was created to address a practical but often overlooked challenge facing professional women chess players: how to continue competing internationally after becoming a mother. “It’s a huge challenge for me to be a mother and at the same time continue competing in chess events. Playing an Olympiad is very important for me: it’s not easy but it can be done thanks to the support of programs such as ChessMom,” said WIM Zenia Corrales, from Mexico. The principle behind the project is straightforward. FIDE provides financial support towards the travel costs of a caregiver accompanying the player and her child, and the expansion has also been visible in the number of beneficiaries. The response to the pilot was overwhelmingly positive. Additionally, for Samarkand 2026, the age limit was extended to children under two, recognising that the practical challenges of combining elite competition and childcare do not disappear after a baby’s first birthday. “The ChessMom project has allowed me to use my time more wisely and to train more effectively. I have realised that becoming a mother doesn’t mean giving up my dreams as a chess player.” – WIM Bayarmaa Bayarjargal (Mongolia) Twelve players from different parts of the world have been selected: GM Marie Sebag (France) GM Elisabeth Pähtz (Germany) WIM Elisabeth Hapala (Austria) WIM Bayarmaa Bayarjargal (Mongolia) WGM Beatriz Irene Franco Valencia (Colombia) WIM Zenia Corrales Jiménez (Mexico) WFM Razan Alshaeby (Jordan) WFM Patricia Evarista Castillo Peña (Dominican Republic) Robyn Julian Klaasen (South Africa) WCM Karen Julissa Figueroa Figueroa (Barbados) WFM Luzia Fernandes Pires (Angola) WIM Onkemetse Linda Francis (Botswana) For the players themselves, the experience is about much more than having a caregiver nearby. It is about being able to remain part of the international chess community during an important stage of both their sporting and personal lives. “It’s very difficult to travel with a baby and keep the motivation to play chess. Motherhood has changed my view on chess in a way – before, when I would lose a game, I would be very upset and now it’s not so important. Even so, when I lose, it’s still not easy to go to sleep!” said GM Marie Sebag (France). Photo: Rafal Oleksiewicz/FIDE The program is very important to mothers: ten years ago, I couldn’t play the Baku Olympiad because my first baby was only three months old,” she added. At the end of the day, ChessMom is built around a simple idea: the chessboard and family life should not have to be competing priorities – motherhood does not have to mark the end of a professional chess journey. One of the mothers, WIM Elisabeth Hapala, from Austria, is married to GM Fernando Peralta, representing Argentina, and both of them are participating in the Olympiad! There is also an important message for the generations coming through behind them. The presence of mothers with their children at one of the world’s largest sporting events demonstrates that a professional chess career does not necessarily have to follow a single path – and that becoming a parent does not have to mean stepping away from elite competition. Written by IM Michael Rahal, FIDE Press Officer (Samarkand)

title: Social Chess Blitz Talks in Samarkand: Stories of freedom, purpose and connection
summary: How can 64 squares become a space for freedom, rehabilitation, communication and human connection? This question was at the heart of the Social Chess Blitz Talks, a new format presented in Samarkand by the FIDE Social Commission. Hosted by Maria Tamkovich, Secretary of the FIDE Social Commission, the session brought together six speakers for a series of short, personal talks highlighting the impact chess can have far beyond competition. From prisons and refugee camps to rehabilitation centres and classrooms, the speakers shared stories of people finding connection, purpose and agency through the game. The event opened with André Vögtlin, Chair of the FIDE Social Commission, who introduced the experimental “Blitz Talk” format: short, focused presentations inspired by the idea of delivering one meaningful message in just a few minutes. The official program described the session as an opportunity to hear “real human stories of transformation,” rather than statistics. Sixty-four squares of freedom In his own talk, Vögtlin explored an apparent contradiction: a chessboard is one of the most restricted spaces imaginable – just 64 squares, fixed rules and clear boundaries – yet within those boundaries people can experience a powerful sense of freedom. He recalled a participant in a prison chess program who, when asked what chess had changed for him, responded not simply that chess made him feel free, but: “I’m freedom, freedom itself.” Vögtlin connected this experience with FIDE Social Commission projects involving prisoners, refugees, seniors and other groups facing different forms of isolation. On the chessboard, he argued, circumstances may remain unchanged, but a person still has the possibility to choose, think independently and take responsibility for a decision. “There is always a move to make” Dana Reizniece, Acting Chair of the FIDE Management Board, continued with stories drawn from social chess initiatives around the world. She recalled bringing chess into a prison in Latvia, where an initially skeptical atmosphere changed once the games began: jokes and noise gave way to concentration, respect and eventually trust. Prison officers who once viewed the initiative cautiously later found themselves supporting the players and rooting for their teams. Reizniece also spoke about working with children with autism, seniors and refugees. She recalled her own visit to the Kakuma refugee camp in Kenya and reflected on how it changed her understanding of hardship and opportunity. For her, the strength of social chess lies not in claiming that the game can magically solve difficult circumstances, but in giving people a space in which they can participate, connect and make their own decisions. “Professional chess touches the brain, but social chess touches the heart and the soul.” She concluded with a simple message: “There is always a move to make.” From personal success to purpose Dr. Das Mukesh, FIDE Social Commission Ambassador and former Executive Director of Indian Oil Corporation, focused on the relationship between a positive mindset and a purposeful one. Drawing on his work with chess programs in Indian prisons, he shared the story of a prisoner serving a life sentence whose involvement with chess developed into competitive achievements and coaching. For Mukesh, the story illustrated how personal transformation can develop further into contribution to others. He presented his concept of moving from “me” to “purpose”: from receiving from society and pursuing individual success toward giving back and finding meaning in the success of others. His central message was that contribution does not have to wait until someone has achieved ideal circumstances. At every stage of life, he argued, there is an opportunity to help another person — whether through a small act, community work or eventually building initiatives capable of wider impact. When the chessboard becomes a language Prabitha Urwyler, FIDE Social Commission Councilor, Treasurer of the European Chess Union and Board member of the Swiss Chess Federation, shared an experience from a social rehabilitation centre in Bulgaria. There she saw therapists using chess not primarily to teach the game, but to help people experiencing psychological crises communicate situations they struggled to express in words. A position on the board could become a representation of a real-life problem: If a piece is under threat, what can it do? Move away? Protect itself? Find another possibility? Ask for help? The same questions could then be transferred to life. “What if the value of chess is sometimes not in learning to play chess at all?” For Urwyler, the experience transformed the chessboard into a language – a physical space where a difficult situation could be placed in front of someone, examined and changed. She left the audience with a question: “What else can these 64 squares become?” Chess as a social bridge Magnus Wolfe Murray, founder and Executive Director of Movement in Refuge, turned the discussion toward displacement, migration and young people. Drawing on his experiences with refugee communities, he contrasted the isolation faced by displaced children with another kind of isolation experienced by some young people in more stable societies. Their circumstances may be radically different, he stressed, but both can lack meaningful contact with people outside their immediate worlds. Chess, he suggested, offers an unusual bridge: it requires little equipment, can cross language barriers and allows two people from completely different circumstances to meet as equals across the same board. “This is not about charity on one side and not on the other. It’s two equals, two opponents, two people who matter to each other.” He stressed that chess cannot solve the global migration crisis, but it can create individual connections – and those connections can matter. The suitcase that carried a life The final Blitz Talk came from Dijana Dengler, Head of Chess at Overseas Family School in Singapore, whose story began with a suitcase. As a young chess player living in Sarajevo, she packed for what she believed would be a four-day tournament: clothes, shoes, two chess books and a chessboard.
